title: On Mercury, the Sun can stop in the sky and move backwards
body: Mercury spins exactly three times for every two orbits of the Sun, a lock set by the Sun’s tides on its stretched, egg-shaped orbit. Combine the slow spin with the fast orbit and a single solar day, sunrise to sunrise, lasts **176 Earth days**, two whole Mercury years. Near its closest approach the planet races along faster than it turns, so for a few Earth days the Sun appears to halt and drift backwards before carrying on.

slides.label: from one sunrise to the next on Mercury, in Earth days
slides.text: A Mercury year is only 88 days, so each solar day lasts two of its years.

slides.alt: Three bars to scale: one rotation, 59 Earth days; one year, 88 Earth days; one solar day, 176 Earth days.
slides.caption: Spin, orbit and solar day, to scale.

slides.heading: Why the Sun reverses
slides.text: Mercury’s orbit is far from circular. Near perihelion it moves so fast that, for a short while, the orbit outpaces the spin. From the surface the Sun seems to stop, back up a little, then resume. At some longitudes it rises, sets and rises again.

slides.heading: A 1965 surprise
slides.text: Until then astronomers assumed Mercury kept one face to the Sun, the way the Moon does to Earth. Radar pulses bounced off the planet in 1965 showed a 59-day spin instead, and revealed the 3:2 rhythm: three spins for every two orbits.

slides.question: Why does the Sun seem to move backwards in Mercury’s sky?
options: Near the Sun, its orbit outruns its spin
slides.explanation: Close to perihelion Mercury moves along its orbit faster than it rotates, so the Sun’s motion across the sky stalls and reverses for a few Earth days.

slides.heading: How long does it take on Mercury?
slides.explanation: Mercury spins three times for every two orbits, and the slow spin plus the fast orbit stretch a solar day to two Mercury years.
